In 2024 REC Silicon had an “unsuccessful qualification test” by its customer (Qcells), followed by the customer communicating that it could no longer wait for delivery of the product to meet those requirements. The company also stated that it had no other U.S. customers and limited customers outside the United States (Norman 2025b, 2025a). 34 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Domestic FBR polysilicon producer REC Silicon maintained a facility for future polysilicon production until 2024, when purity concerns caused cancellation of its primary remaining supply agreement with Qcells, its largest shareholder (Norman 2025b, 2025a). This represents an 8.8- GW decline in U.S. polysilicon capacity from 2024 to 2025. With cancellation of the REC dc Silicon contract, Qcells announced in January 2025 that it would procure polysilicon from OCI Holdings’ factory in Malaysia for its U.S. wafer manufacturing operations in Georgia (Samora 2025). The REC Silicon facility in Moses Lake, Washington, switched to serving the battery supply chain. The silane intermediate it produces can be used to make higher-energy-density battery anodes, and the company has entered into a long-term agreement to supply U.S.- headquartered battery materials supplier Sila beginning in 2025 (REC Silicon 2024).28 At the same time, U.S.-headquartered Highland Materials announced it could begin constucting an 8- GW -equivalent polysilicon facility in Tennessee in 2026 (Jacobo 2025b). dc As shown in Figure 23, Hemlock and Wacker combined could offer up to 31 GW of dc polysilicon capacity to PV. Historically, however, the semiconductor industry has paid higher average selling prices for polysilicon and has provided more stability in offtake agreements with customers. As of Q2 2025, Corning (7 GW ) and Qcells (3 GW ) had the only U.S. ingot and dc dc wafer plants under construction, which could demand U.S. PV polysilicon (see Section 2.5.2).
